steps.title: Two people organising an open day
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 129 words · informal messages

— Just got the list. Bicentenary open day, the 14th. You free?

— Should be. Doing what?

— Two of us on the door, one in the aircraft hall. They've put the monoplane back in.

— The multicoloured one? Thought that was illegal to fly.

— It is. Static display only.

— Fine. Bilingual signs done?

— Being printed. Chairs arriving Tuesday. They want them in a semicircle round the plane.

— How many?

— Sixty. Not enough. Told them twice.

— Parking?

— Main car park open from nine. Barrier still broken. Reported it twice as well.

— And the talk?

— Half three. Speaker's semi-retired, apparently, so it shouldn't run long.

— Monotone?

— Hope not. Last one nearly finished me.

— Right. See you Tuesday, then. Bring the tape measure.

steps.title: Two hundred years of flight — open day, 14 June
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 143 words · the museum's notice

The museum's bicentenary falls this year, and our biannual open day will mark it. Admission is free and all signs are bilingual.

The centrepiece is the restored monoplane, given to us in 1974 by a multimillionaire collector who had flown it on an early intercontinental attempt. It has not left the hall since.

Two galleries reopen on the same day. The first traces how early airfields came to interconnect across Europe. The second displays the semi-human figures carved into the museum's original doors, which visitors ask about constantly and which have nothing to do with aviation at all.

Chairs will be arranged in a semicircle for the afternoon talk, which begins at half past three. Photography is permitted throughout. Flying any aircraft over the site is illegal and will be reported.

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.sub: The text argues that a reader who stops at every unknown word reads more slowly and understands less.
steps.prompt: Why should stopping less often produce better understanding, not just faster reading?
options: Because the unknown words are usually unimportant ones.
Because meaning is carried by whole sentences, and a reader who keeps going still has the sentence to work with.
Because dictionaries are often wrong about the sense in context.
steps.answer: Because meaning is carried by whole sentences, and a reader who keeps going still has the sentence to work with.
steps.why: The claim is not that the word does not matter. It is that the context around it is the evidence, and stopping throws that evidence away.

steps.sub: A prefix changes meaning without changing the word class: legal and illegal are both adjectives.
steps.prompt: What follows from that for a reader meeting an unfamiliar word?
options: The prefix tells you what part of speech the word belongs to.
If you recognise the stem, the prefix usually tells you the direction of the meaning while the grammar stays the same.
Words carrying a prefix are negative in almost every case.
steps.answer: If you recognise the stem, the prefix usually tells you the direction of the meaning while the grammar stays the same.
steps.why: This is why prefixes are worth learning as a set: they multiply what you can read, not just what you can say.

steps.title: Reading a word you have never met
steps.html:
Two things at once: how a prefix changes a word, and what informal writing leaves out.

A prefix carries its own meaning and does not change the word class. Legal and illegal are both adjectives; connect and interconnect are both verbs. If you know the prefix, you can read the word.

The quantity prefixes are the ones this lesson's wordlist is built on: bi- (two), mono- (one), multi- (many), semi- (half), inter- (between).

The negative prefixes are un-, in-, dis-, and mis-. In- changes shape to fit the sound after it: il- before l (illegal), im- before m or p (impossible), ir- before r (irresponsible).

Mis- is not simply negative. It means wrongly or badly: misunderstand is not the opposite of understand — it is understanding the wrong thing.

steps.title: Reading an unfamiliar word from its parts
steps.html:
1. You meet the word intercontinental for the first time.
  2. Take off the prefix: inter-. From the table, it means between.
  3. What is left is continental, from continent. So the word means between continents.
  4. Check the word class. Continental is an adjective, and a prefix does not change the class, so intercontinental is an adjective: an intercontinental flight.
  5. Now do the same with illegible: il- = not, legible = able to be read → impossible to read, adjective.

steps.title: You are going to turn a set of messages into a formal notice.
Write the notice.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Nothing may be left out — every sentence complete. Use at least five prefixed words.
steps.html:
• Open with what the event is and when.
  • Describe the main attraction in full sentences.
  • Add one detail that visitors always ask about.
  • Finish with a practical instruction and one prohibition.

Useful language

  • The … falls this year, and our biannual … will mark it.
  • Admission is free and all signs are bilingual.
  • The centrepiece is …
  • Chairs will be arranged in a semicircle for …
  • Photography is permitted throughout.
  • … is illegal and will be reported.
steps.modelHtml:
Norwood Rowing Club — 150 years, 6 September

The club's anniversary falls this year, and our biannual open day will mark it. Admission is free, and all signs and programmes are bilingual.

The centrepiece is the restored 1908 four, given to the club in 1991 by a multimillionaire former member. It has not been on the water since, and it will not be going on the water on Saturday either.

Two rooms reopen on the same day. The first traces how the river clubs came to interconnect in the 1890s. The second displays the multicoloured racing blades of every crew since 1912, along with the semi-human figure carved above the boathouse door, which nobody has ever been able to explain.

Chairs will be arranged in a semicircle for the afternoon talk at half past three. Swimming from the landing stage is illegal and will be reported.
